newsitem.title: UK: British markets applaud preventative rate medicine.
newsitem.headline: British markets applaud preventative rate medicine.

text.p: British markets saw the bright side of a surprise quarter-point rise in British interest rates on Wednesday, applauding Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's anti-inflation stance.

Sterling rose more than a pfennig against the mark, the FTSE 100 index of leading shares bounced off its lows, and the British bond market was expected to perform well in the medium-term after initial mild losses on Wednesday.
The move, which pushed British base rates up to six percent, caught markets off guard as many did not expect Clarke to risk a vote-losing rate rise before a general election.
But analysts said the timing of the move was shrewd.

"It's not necessarily bad news. It's far enough away from the election for the electorate to forget about it. Damage will be limited," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Investment Bank in London.
Prime Minister John Major must call an election by May 22, 1997, although he said earlier this month that the election would be no later than May 1.
Sterling rose to 22-month highs at 2.4637/42 marks at 1303 GMT from just below 2.45 before the interest rate move was announced. It climbed to $1.6338/48 from $1.6200 beforehand.
The FTSE 100 stabilised at 3977.4, down 16.1 points from the prior close.
December gilt futures fell to 109-23, down 2/32 from the previous close and off from 110-00 before the rate news. But analysts said the British bond market was poised to strengthen.

"It limits the size of any rate rise that may be needed in the near future. By moving quickly now it limits the damage we could expect if he waited," said Tim Fox, international economist at Standard Chartered in London.

The immediate focus would now turn to Britain's November 26 budget, and analysts said the one potential downside to Wedneday's move was that Clarke would take advantage of the monetary tightening to loosen fiscal policy.
Clarke is under political pressure from the ruling Conservative Party to deliver large tax give-aways in the budget in the hope of swaying votors before the election.
"From the markets' point of view, the most likely scenario is that Labour will win and the rate rise won't immediately change that," said Rob Hayward, economist at BankAmerica in London.
Clarke, in announcing the credit tightening, said he would not jeopardise Britain's inflation achievements.

"The economy is performing exceptionally well," he said in a statement. "We have delivered a combination of healthy growth and sustained low inflation unseen for a generation. I am determined to maintain a firm grip on inflation to sustain this well into the future."
While the markets welcomed the preventative nature of the rate increase, analysts said it was still possible Clarke could tighten monetary policy before the election.
British short-sterling futures for March 1997, which reflect market expectations for interest rates at that time, were at 93.59, down 17 basis points from Tuesday's close.
That implies three-month interest rates of around 6.40 percent.
